_README: Adversarial frame-decode vectors, shared by all three SDKs.
Every SDK validates magic, version, reserved bytes, reserved flag bits,
both CRC32Cs and the payload-length bound. That code is written three
times and, until this file existed, exercised zero times -- it is the
layer that protects a client from a hostile or buggy peer, and a client
SDK reads bytes it did not produce by definition.
Cases are declarative so all three build byte-identical input: start from
a valid frame, apply one mutation, expect one error. A runner that cannot
reproduce the bytes fails rather than skipping.
Header layout (32 bytes, big-endian):
0..4 magic 'BRN0' | 4 version | 5..7 opcode | 7 flags
8..12 header_crc32c (over 0..8 ++ 12..32) | 12..16 stream_id
16..19 payload_len (u24) | 19 reserved_a | 20..24 payload_crc32c
24..32 reserved_b
`expect` names the shared error taxonomy: BadMagic, BadVersion,
BadHeaderCrc, BadPayloadCrc, OversizePayload, ReservedNonZero, Truncated.
Mutations are applied AFTER the frame is encoded, so header_crc is
already correct for the unmutated bytes. Any mutation inside the CRC's
coverage therefore also invalidates the header CRC -- which is why the
cases below expect BadHeaderCrc where that is what a decoder checks
first. `recrc: true` re-computes the header CRC after mutating, to reach
the check that the case is actually about.

cases.name: bad_magic
cases.why: First four bytes are the frame sentinel; a wrong one means the stream is not BRN0 at all.

cases.name: bad_version
cases.why: A future wire version must be refused, not guessed at.

cases.name: reserved_a_nonzero
cases.why: Reserved header byte 19 is a forward-compat slot; a non-zero value means the peer is speaking something this version cannot interpret.

cases.name: reserved_flag_bit
cases.why: Only EOS/MPL/CMP are defined; an undefined flag bit is not ignorable, because a later version may give it meaning that changes framing.

cases.name: header_crc_flipped
cases.why: A single flipped bit anywhere in the header must be caught before any field is trusted.

cases.name: stream_id_tampered
cases.why: stream_id sits inside the header CRC's coverage; tampering routes a reply to the wrong waiter, so it must not pass.

cases.name: payload_crc_flipped
cases.why: Payload corruption is invisible to the header CRC; the second checksum is the only thing that catches it.

cases.name: payload_byte_corrupted
cases.why: The realistic corruption case: header intact, one payload byte flipped in transit.

cases.name: truncated_header
cases.why: A short read must ask for more bytes, never index past the buffer.

cases.name: truncated_payload
cases.why: Header declares more payload than arrived -- the classic split-read. Must be Truncated (read more), not a CRC failure.

cases.name: oversize_payload_len
cases.why: A hostile length must be rejected BEFORE a buffer is reserved for it, or the length alone is an allocation attack. u24 max is 16 MiB; this claims all of it while sending none.

cbor_cases.name: deeply_nested_arrays
cbor_cases.why: CVE-2026-26209 in cbor2: uncontrolled recursion let a <100KB payload crash the process. Every SDK must bound this, by an explicit depth cap or by catching the overflow -- what it must not do is die.

cbor_cases.name: trailing_bytes_after_item
cbor_cases.why: A complete CBOR item followed by garbage means the framing and the payload disagree; the server rejects this too.

cbor_cases.name: truncated_cbor_item
cbor_cases.why: A map header promising two pairs with none following must not read past the buffer.

cbor_cases.name: indefinite_length_map
cbor_cases.why: Brain's encoder is deterministic and never emits indefinite-length items; accepting one from a peer means accepting bytes the corpus can never pin.
